o: **Understanding the problem**: s is some concatenation t₁t₂…t_k of anagrams of one string t; find the minimum possible |t|. |t| must divide |s|, and every block of that length must be an anagram of the first block (identical multisets). Testing a candidate length ℓ costs O(|s|) with per-block character counts, and divisors can be tried in increasing order, returning the first success. Examples: "abba" → 2 ("ba","ab"); "cdef" → 4 (only itself); "abcbcacabbaccba" → 3.
k: |t| must be a divisor of n = |s|, and validity = all n/ℓ blocks share one character-frequency signature.
Trying divisors in ascending order and returning the first valid one is correct because smaller valid lengths always exist independently of larger ones.

a.n: Approach 1: Try divisors in ascending order with count signatures
a.i: For each divisor ℓ of n (ascending), compute the count vector of the first block and verify every other block matches. First success is the answer; ℓ = n always succeeds.
s: Enumerate divisors of n in ascending order.
For each ℓ, build the 26-count signature of s[0..ℓ).
For each subsequent block, recount and compare; if all match, return ℓ.
a.t: O(n·d(n)) — each divisor costs O(n) to verify, and n has at most ~134 divisors for n ≤ 10⁵

a.i: Instead of recounting each block, hash each block's canonical signature (e.g., polynomial hash of the sorted-count encoding, or a commutative hash like Σ hash(digit)·count) so blocks compare in O(1). Useful when the alphabet or block recount is expensive.
s: Precompute per-position prefix structures allowing O(1) block signature extraction (e.g., prefix counts per letter give O(26) extraction, or commit to a randomized commutative hash for O(1)).
Enumerate divisors ascending; compare all block signatures to the first block's.
a.t: O(n·d(n)) expected — O(1) signature comparison per block via prefix sums (randomization guards against collisions)

w: **Wrap-up**: Approach 1 is deterministic and plenty fast; reach for hashing only if block recounts become the bottleneck (huge alphabets). Pitfalls: forgetting ℓ must divide n, and that ℓ = n is always a valid fallback. Note the sum of all letters per block is automatically equal when signatures match — no separate length check needed. Follow-ups: count all valid t lengths, or handle the case where blocks may be anagrams of *different* strings (then the problem changes fundamentally).
